A fistful of upright reed slivers pushed into a cork-bark base at different angles, each sliver leaning toward the star it tracks, the whole cluster tilting like a crowd turning their faces at once; one sliver has been nudged crooked and she is nudging it straight with a fingernail.

A broad pale mushroom gill-plate laid face-up with luminous amber seeds pressed one by one along its ridges, each ridge a different distance from centre, the count on the longest ridge showing the brightest arc; a violet beetle is trundling slowly across the outermost ridge, displacing three of them and entirely unaware.

A floating cork disc on a cupped dish of still water, one thorn standing upright at its middle, the disc turning itself on the current until the thorn's shadow falls exactly across a star reflected below it; a single copper-coloured moth rests on the dish's rim, wings flat open.

A fan of twelve stiff owl-feather shafts spread in the hand, each shaft angled out to match a star of the group, the spacing between them carrying the shape of the whole arc, the narrowest gap held open by a sliver of thorn jammed in.

A net of dried grass stems strung between two forked hazel twigs, the whole mesh beaded over with dewdrops, held up at arm's length so each drop sits over one star and swells it huge; the bottom-left corner of the net is coming loose and three drops have run together.

Two polished river pebbles threaded on a single grass cord, slid apart until the gap between them spans exactly the width of two wandering stars, then pinched tight and brought down to compare against a row of waiting pebbles on a flat stone below.

A cage of five nested rings cut from elder-wood, each ring hung with a single coloured seed on a thread of milkweed floss, the rings turned by hand so the seeds orbit each other in shrinking loops; the innermost seed is wound tight and beginning to spin back the other way.

A hollow reed held at arm's length, one eye closed, the other looking straight down its throat where a single star fills the whole bore; a grass cord tied around the reed holds the exact angle where the star sat an hour ago.

A spiral of graduated snail shells laid out across a flat river stone, the smallest at the centre, the largest at the outer coil, the distance each shell sits from the middle showing how far from the pole each star wanders; the largest shell has been placed upside down by accident and is being righted.

A row of fourteen upright grass cords pegged into moss in a shallow arc, each cord carrying one polished seed slid to a different height, read by dropping the cheek almost to the ground until every seed aligns on its own star behind; the fourth cord is bowing sideways under a heavier bead than the rest.

A sheet of pond ice the size of a spread hand, holes melted through it in a careful scatter by a warmed thorn, held up against the sky so each pinprick glows with its own real star perfectly framed; one hole at the edge is slightly oval where the thorn slipped.

A broad leaf held face-up to the moon, pinpricks through its surface letting the light fall as hard bright points on the stone below, the pattern of points matching the overhead arc; a crumb of pine resin plugs one hole that was pricked one degree wrong.

A shallow tray of fine river sand laid flat, small quartz pebbles pressed into it at the positions of a moving group, the dents holding all night; a dormouse has walked one curious path across a corner of the tray and the prints are being worked around and left exactly where they are.

A dewdrop cradled in a tight ring of bent grass, held out at arm's length on a long stem so that one star swells into the whole curved belly of the drop; a second drop clinging to the grass ring beneath it shows the same star small and upside down.

A length of grass cord knotted once for every night since a wandering star first appeared, hung taut between two twig pegs, the newest knot still loose and warm from her fingers, the oldest knots compressed into a firm ridge near the left-hand peg.

A slab of soft cork bark with long hawthorn thorns pushed in at different depths across its face, the tallest for the brightest star, the shortest barely showing above the surface, the whole relief read by tilting the slab until the thorn-tips all catch the same raking light.

A cupped dish of still water set on a flat stone, the whole sky doubled on its surface, stars lying perfectly underfoot; an apricot-veined moth has landed at the centre of the reflection and with its wings open covers the three stars she needs most, to her considerable disgust.

Glow-worms coaxed one at a time onto a square of velvet moss until their cold green lights reproduce the shape of the group above, each worm's position read by looking straight up then straight down; two have wandered nearly a finger's-width out of true and one is being carried back on a leaf scrap.

A hoop of bent green willow with a single luminous seed hanging on a hair-fine grass fibre at its exact centre, held out at arm's length and tilted until the seed hangs precisely over one chosen star; the hoop's join is lashed with three tight wraps of grass cord, the last wrap still bright-pale and fresh.

A disc of thin cork bark with river pebbles laid on its surface in two concentric rings, the inner ring count for stars already passed, the outer for stars yet to rise, spun slowly with one finger so the rings rotate around the fixed thorn at its hub; one pebble has drifted between the rings and nobody is sure which count it belongs to.

A long grass cord strung between two twig posts, with coloured seeds knotted onto it at intervals, each seed's colour belonging to a different wandering star, its position along the cord showing the night it last came round; the cord sags slightly in the middle from the weight of six seeds clustered there.

A fan of broad lichen fronds held edge-on in a spread grip, each frond a slightly different length, the stepped heights across the fan matching the brightness rank of a row of stars from brightest to least; a snail is crossing the longest frond serenely indifferent to the work it is interrupting.

A pair of joined hazel twigs hinged at one end with a grass lashing, spread open until the gap at the tips matches exactly the angular distance between two stars, then laid carefully flat on a moss pad where two waiting pins stand at the gap she got last night; the hinge is tighter on one side than the other.

A shallow bone-white acorn cap filled with still water to the exact brim, the curved surface bowing up, a single star reflected and magnified in the meniscus at the centre; she holds it in both cupped hands because the slightest tilt spills the star entirely off the edge.

A length of dried river reed split into eleven slivers of unequal length, bound at the base into a bundle, the slivers fanning out like organ pipes, each one stopped at a different height by a bead of pine resin that sets that height as a count; she is pressing a warm thumbnail into a fresh resin bead to fix the last one.

A row of tall thorns pushed upright into a slab of soft cork bark, each thorn standing at a different height, the taller the thorn the brighter the star it holds, one thorn leaning badly and propped back plumb with a wedge of acorn cap.

A cupped dish of still water with a floating disc of cork carrying a single upright pin, the pin turning slowly as the reflected star it tracks drifts across the surface, a water-boatman crossing the far edge of the sky underneath.

A broad pale mushroom gill-plate laid horizontal, luminous seeds pressed one by one along the ridges in the exact spacing of the group overhead, two seeds rolled together into the wrong groove and being nudged apart with a grass stem.

A hoop of bent willow with a single amber-coloured seed hung on a grass-fibre thread at its centre, held out at arm's length until the seed swings still and sits exactly over the star, the thread still shivering from the last adjustment.

A fan of seven stiff owl-feather shafts spread across the moss, each shaft angled to match one bright star of the group, the gaps between them holding the same proportions as the sky, the outermost shaft slipping and being caught with a knee.

A spiral of snail shells laid out from the centre of a flat stone outward, the smallest shell nearest the middle for the faintest star, the largest on the outside for the brightest, one shell still occupied and dragging itself half a length off course.

A net of fine grass stems strung between two forked twigs and beaded all over with dew, held up at arms length so each drop sits over its own star and doubles it, one drop gone milky with cold and blotting its star entirely.

A shallow tray of fine river-sand with river pebbles pressed into it at the positions of the group overhead, the dents holding the pattern through the night, a beetle walking the rim and stopping to investigate the largest pebble with its antennae.

Two polished seeds on a single moss-cord thread, slid apart until the gap between them matches the gap between the two stars being measured, then pinched tight and carried level across to the reference stone without breathing hard enough to shift them.

A hollow reed held to one eye, shutting out every star but the one burning at its far end, the fae rotating it slowly until the star sits dead centre, a moth settled on the near end with wings flat and refusing to move.

A sheet of clear pond ice with holes melted through it by a warmed thorn tip, each hole admitting one star as a hard bright point, held up in both hands and tilted until every point aligns, a crack running through three of them already.

A broad leaf stretched flat and held up to the moon, holes pricked through it in the pattern of the group, the moonlight arriving on the moss below as a scatter of fierce bright points, one hole plugged with pine resin because it was pricked crooked.

River pebbles laid out on a mossy stone in a pattern matching the group overhead, the bigger the pebble the brighter the star, a snail crossing the arrangement with its shell nudging the second-largest pebble a full body-length out of true.

A cage of five nested carved-wood rings, each carrying one coloured seed on a moss-cord loop, turned slowly by hand so the seeds swing past each other in their proper paths, the outermost ring lashed with fresh grass-cord where it split last season.

A dewdrop held steady in a ring of bent grass, one eye brought close until a single star swells huge inside it, the image trembling every time the holder breathes, a second dewdrop forming on the ring itself and being flicked away with a thumbnail.

A row of upright grass cords pegged into a pad of moss, each cord carrying one polished amber bead slid to its own height, read by dropping low until every bead lines up with its star, the tallest cord bowing gently under the bead's weight.

Glow-worms coaxed one at a time onto a cushion of deep moss until they hold the same pattern as the group overhead, two already drifting from position, a third being ferried back on a curled leaf held flat so its light does not tip out.

A broad flat stone with a long row of river pebbles counted out along one edge, one pebble added for each night since the comet rose, the newest pebble still wet from the stream and darker than all the rest.

A grass cord knotted once for every night since the wandering star shifted course, each knot a different distance from the last to show how far it moved, the final knot still loose and being tightened between finger and thumb right now.

A length of moss-cord strung between two upright thorns, threaded with coloured seeds at intervals, each colour standing for a different wandering star, each position along the cord showing where that star sits tonight, one seed still spinning from being placed.

A disc of pale birch bark crowded with brass-bright pins, coloured reed-fibre threads strung taut between them so the thread pattern is the constellation entire, one thread gone slack where its pin pulled loose and hanging free in the cool air.

A cupped half-shell of walnut set on a stone with still water filling it to the brim, the relevant stars doubled and laid flat on the surface, the fae leaning over until her own reflection swallows the whole eastern quarter by accident.

A ring of bent willow laid flat on the moss with river pebbles placed around its inner edge at intervals, each pebble's position around the circle showing where a star rises tonight, one pebble tipped on its side and not yet noticed.

A cone of rolled birch bark open at both ends, held up so one bright star at a time can be drawn down its throat and centred by eye, the inner surface furred with lichen so the star arrives alone against deep green.

A pad of moss with short thorns pushed in at positions matching the overhead group, fine dandelion-down threads pulled taut between them to show which stars belong to the same shape, the whole thing trembling because it is balanced on an acorn cup as a pivot.

A loose weave of flat grass blades laid over a stone, each blade crossing the others at the angle of a different star pair, the crossings showing their meeting-points, one blade sliding out of place and being pressed back with a careful elbow.

A deep hollow carved into a rounded river pebble, filled with still water, the star it watches doubled at the bottom of the bowl, the fae tipping the pebble until the reflection sits exactly over the carved notch at the rim that marks last season.

A length of bark strip with long grass-fibre threads hanging from it like a fringe, each thread weighted at its end with a river pebble of a different size, the threads swinging at different lengths and being read where they cross each other in the air.

A flat stone with concentric rings of river pebbles pressed into soft moss on its surface, each ring a different distance from the centre, each pebble on its ring standing for one night's position of the wandering star, the outermost ring not yet finished.

A bundle of reeds cut to different lengths and bound side by side, each reed open at its top, the fae blowing softly across them until the one tuned to the right angle of the sky hums, locating the star by which reed resonates under her cheek.

A row of thorns pushed upright into a strip of soft cork bark at different heights, the tallest for the brightest star, read by tilting the bark until each tip lines up with its own point overhead, one thorn leaning where the cork has dried and split.

A cupped half-acorn shell filled to the brim with still water, the whole group of five wandering stars doubled on its surface in miniature, a long-limbed hand keeping it level while it trembles on the edge of spilling.

A fan of stiff primary feathers spread open, each shaft angled outward to match the spacing of a bright group above, held at arm's length against the sky, one feather sliding loose and being caught between two knees before it falls.
A grass cord knotted at uneven intervals, one knot per night since the comet first showed, the earliest knots tight and amber-stained, the last one still loose and warm from being tied just now.

A broad pale mushroom gill-plate laid flat with one luminous seed pressed into each gill-ridge at a different distance from the centre, the distance encoding how far each wandering star sits from the fixed group, a beetle walking the outermost ridge and nudging one seed sideways.

A net of fine moss-cord strung between two peeled willow twigs and beaded all over with dew, each drop sitting directly over one star when the net is raised and tilted, one drop gone milky with cold and blurring the star behind it.

A spiral of snail shells laid out from the centre of a flat stone outward, each shell one night's measured position of a wandering star, a long-fingered hand pressing the newest shell into place while the previous one still rocks.

A hollow reed held vertically and looked down through, shutting out every star but the single brilliant one framed at its far end, the reed balanced on one fingertip while the other hand steadies a second reed beside it for the next star.

A shallow tray of fine river sand with rounded pebbles pressed into it at different depths, the deeper the press the brighter the star, carried two-handed across a mossy flat with visible effort to keep the whole arrangement from shifting.

A cage of five nested carved-wood rings, each hung with a single coloured seed on a moss-cord thread, turned by one hand so the violet seed and the amber seed swing close and then apart, one outer ring mended with a knot of split reed fibre where it cracked.

A single broad leaf held up to the moon with dozens of holes pricked through it, moonlight pouring through in a hard scatter of bright points, one hole plugged with a pressed crumb of pine resin because it landed in the wrong place.

A hoop of bent willow with a single apricot-coloured seed hung at its centre on a thread of milkweed floss, held out at arm's length while the eye lines seed against star, the hoop tilted and corrected and tilted again.

River pebbles arranged on a mossy stone in a long curving line, each pebble one star, the largest a smooth river cobble nearly too big to carry, the smallest a chip of quartz, a snail crossing the whole arrangement and lifting two of them slightly on its foot.

A sheet of pond ice with pinprick holes melted through by a warmed thorn, each hole admitting one star's light, the ice held at a careful arm's length with both hands while meltwater runs down both wrists.

A floating disc of cork bark on a dish of still water with a single upright thorn at its centre, the disc turning slowly as it follows the current of a breath, a second thorn laid across the rim as a counter-weight to keep it even.

Two amber seeds on a single thread of dandelion-down fibre, slid apart until the gap between them matches the gap between two stars, then held rigid against the sky with both thumbs pressing the seeds in place so they cannot drift.

A broad pad of deep emerald moss crowded with brass-bright pins, coloured threads of split reed fibre strung taut between them in a hard-edged shape that is itself the group overhead, a moth asleep on the moss with wings spread flat across three threads and pressing them gently out of true.

Eleven upright grass cords pegged into a moss strip, each with one polished river bead slid to a different height, the whole row read by dropping one cheek to the ground until every bead sits on its own star, the tallest cord bowing faintly under its bead's weight.

A dewdrop cradled in a ring of bent grass and held up to a single star, the star swelling enormous inside the drop, one finger of the steadying hand trembling with the effort of keeping it still long enough to read.

Glow-worms coaxed one at a time onto a cushion of deep violet moss until they stand in the same pattern as the group overhead, two already wandering and a third being carried back on a curved leaf, the whole cushion humming faintly with their cold green light.

A fan of overlapping fish scales pinned at one edge onto a bark slab, each scale lifted to a different angle on a thorn-pivot, the angle encoding each star's height above the horizon, one scale missing and replaced by a fragment of pale lichen held at the right angle by a drop of pine resin.

A row of snail shells stood upright in a line on a flat stone, each tipped to a different angle of lean, the lean itself the position of a star along the horizon, one shell tipped so far it has fallen and rolled to the stone's edge.

A length of grass cord wound in a tight coil, each loop a different colour of plant-dye, each colour one of the wandering stars at one counted position, unwound finger by finger in sequence to show the path a star has taken across many nights.

A broad bracket fungus used as a flat working surface covered entirely with short upright grass-stem pins, the count in each cluster encoding the number of nights a star spent in each position, a dormouse asleep across one whole cluster and flattening six of them.

A pinched clay bowl no wider than a cupped palm, filled with still water and set on the flattest stone available, a complete group of bright stars lying doubled on the surface, one petal drifting in and blotting three of them entirely while a hand reaches to fish it out.

A length of peeled willow with notch-free but colour-coded rings of wound grass at uneven intervals along it, each ring's distance from the last encoding how many nights apart two events fell, held up beside the sky with one eye closed.

A long trailing grass cord strung between two twig-pegs with coloured seeds threaded onto it, each seed at a measured position along the cord, the cord's curve itself the path the wandering star has taken, one seed still sliding down toward its neighbour under gravity.

A small flat stone balanced on a rolled bark cylinder so it tilts freely in any direction, a single thorn upright at the centre, the angle of the thorn's shadow from a low ember replaced by the thorn's own alignment to a star, a hand pressing one edge of the stone down to correct the tilt.

A collection of river pebbles sorted into three groups by size on a moss pad — large for the three brightest, middle for the next group, small for the barely visible ones — the groups being shuffled urgently as a cloud passes and the ranking suddenly seems wrong.

A hollow seed-pod with a single pinprick hole at one end and a pad of damp white pith at the other, held up so one star's light travels through the hole and lands as a bright point on the pith, the position of that point on the pith showing the star's exact height, one hand shaking slightly with cold.

A flat slab of cork bark furred all over with short thorns pushed in at different depths, the tallest standing for the brightest stars, coloured seeds threaded down each thorn to its set height, one seed still spinning where her fingertip just released it.

A row of fourteen upright reed slivers pegged into soft ground, each with a single amber bead slid to its own height, the whole row read by pressing one cheek to the moss until every bead sits exactly over its own star, the shortest reed vibrating faintly.

A broad pale mushroom gill-plate laid across both palms, luminous green seeds pressed one by one into the ridges so their glow marks the position of each wandering star, a snail crossing the far edge and nudging the outermost seed a full ridge sideways.

A cupped acorn-cap dish of still water balanced on a flat stone, the sky lying doubled and underfoot in it, a moth settling at the rim with wings spread so its shadow blots out four reflected stars and she is blowing at it very gently.

A fan of eleven stiff owl-feather shafts bound at their quills with moss-cord and spread to match the exact spacing of a group overhead, read by holding the fan at arm's length and rotating until every shaft tip sits on its own star, one shaft cracked.

A cage of four nested carved-alder rings, each hung with a single coloured seed on a hair-fine grass fibre, turned by hand so the seeds orbit each other in arcs that match the wandering stars, the innermost ring still warm where she carved it tonight.

A shallow tray of fine river sand with river pebbles pressed into it at the positions of each star, the bigger the pebble the brighter the star, carried flat so the dents hold overnight, one large pebble rolled and left a groove the length of her thumb.

A net of dried grass stems strung taut between two forked twigs and hung all over with dew-beads, held up so each drop sits over its own star and doubles it, one bead gone milky with cold and swelling huge around a star it cannot name.

A hollow reed held upright, looked down through its bore so every other star is shut away and only one burns at the bottom of the dark tunnel, the end of the reed still wet where she cut it an hour ago with her nail.

A hoop of bent willow as wide as a spread hand, a single rose-hip hung on a milkweed-floss thread at its exact centre, held out at arm's length until the hip covers one wandering star and the hoop frames the five around it, her elbow shaking slightly.

A grass cord knotted once for every night since the comet rose, forty-one knots now, the newest still loose and warm, an earlier knot unpicked and retied tighter because she miscounted, the whole cord looped twice around her wrist to keep it taut while she works.

A sheet of pond ice the size of two palms, holes melted through at each star's position by a warmed thorn, held up to the sky so cold light pours through in hard points, a crack running between two holes that were not meant to be neighbours.

Glow-worms coaxed onto a cushion of deep moss until they stand in the same pattern as the group overhead, four placed correctly and two already wandering, a third being ferried back on a rolled leaf by someone moving with the care of someone who has done this before.

A spiral of snail shells laid out from the centre of a mossy stone outward, each shell one night's position of a wandering star along its track, the freshest shell still damp, placed just now, a beetle walking the spiral inward as though reading it back.

Two polished river seeds on a single milkweed-floss thread, slid apart until the gap between them exactly matches the gap between two stars, the thread then pinched and held very still while she memorises the span with the width of her own fingers as a bridge.
